name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q20 - Reaction of toluene with chlorine in dark with iron

questiontext.text: The reaction of toluene with chlorine in the presence of iron and in the absence of light yields

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electrophilic aromatic substitution occurs when toluene reacts with chlorine in the presence of an iron catalyst (\(\mathrm{Fe}\), which forms \(\mathrm{FeCl}_3\) in situ) in the absence of light. Under these conditions, free-radical side-chain halogenation is suppressed, and ring chlorination is favoured.

Step 2: Directing Effect of the Methyl Group
The methyl group (\(\mathrm{-CH}_3\)) attached to the benzene ring is electron-donating via inductive (+I) and hyperconjugation effects, activating the benzene ring and directing the incoming chloronium electrophile (\(\mathrm{Cl}^+\)) preferentially to the ortho and para positions.

Step 3: Product Formation
Electrophilic substitution at the ortho and para positions yields a mixture of both o-chlorotoluene and p-chlorotoluene. Benzyl chloride is not formed because benzylic side-chain substitution requires light or high temperature to generate radicals.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The reaction yields a mixture of o-chlorotoluene and p-chlorotoluene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q21 - Reaction of chloromethane with excess ammonia

questiontext.text: Chloromethane on treatment with excess of ammonia yields mainly

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In Hofmann's ammonolysis of alkyl halides, ammonia acts as a nucleophile to displace the halide ion, initially generating a primary amine. The primary amine itself possesses a lone pair of electrons and can act as a nucleophile to react with remaining alkyl halide, leading successively to secondary and tertiary amines, and eventually quaternary ammonium salts.

Step 2: Effect of Reagent Proportions
When ammonia is present in large excess relative to chloromethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{Cl}\)), the probability of a chloromethane molecule colliding with an ammonia molecule is overwhelmingly higher than colliding with an already formed primary amine molecule. Consequently, further alkylation is suppressed.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Under conditions of excess ammonia, the reaction predominantly halts at the primary amine stage, yielding methanamine (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{NH}_2\)) as the major product.

answer.text: Mixture containing all these in equal proportion

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q22 - Identification of chiral haloalkane molecule

questiontext.text: Molecules whose mirror image is non superimposable over them are known as chiral. Which of the following molecules is chiral in nature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A molecule is chiral if it lacks an alternating axis of symmetry (most commonly planes or centres of symmetry) and possesses a non-superimposable mirror image. In organic chemistry, a tetrahedral carbon atom bonded to four entirely different atoms or groups is an asymmetric (chiral) centre, conferring chirality to simple mono-haloalkanes.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Structures
- 2-Bromobutane: The carbon atom at position 2 is bonded to four distinct groups: a methyl group (\(\mathrm{-CH}_3\)), an ethyl group (\(\mathrm{-CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\)), a hydrogen atom (\(\mathrm{-H}\)), and a bromine atom (\(\mathrm{-Br}\)). Because all four substituents are different, this carbon is chiral, making the molecule chiral.
- 1-Bromobutane: Carbon-1 is bonded to two identical hydrogen atoms; hence it is achiral.
- 2-Bromopropane: Carbon-2 is bonded to two identical methyl groups; hence it is achiral.
- 2-Bromopropan-2-ol: Carbon-2 is bonded to two identical methyl groups; hence it is achiral.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The chiral molecule is 2-bromobutane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q23 - Mechanism of hydrolysis of benzyl bromide

questiontext.text: Reaction of \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Br}\) with aqueous sodium hydroxide follows

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The mechanism of nucleophilic substitution depends fundamentally on the stability of the carbocation that can be generated upon departure of the leaving group. When an exceptionally stable carbocation can be formed, unimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N1}\)) is strongly promoted.

Step 2: Analysis of the Intermediate
Heterolytic cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond in benzyl bromide (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\)) produces the benzyl carbocation (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\overset{+}{\mathrm{C}}\mathrm{H}_2\)). The positive charge on the benzylic carbon is extensively delocalized throughout the conjugated \(\pi\)-system of the aromatic ring across several resonance structures, providing outstanding stability to this carbocation intermediate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Due to the exceptional resonance stabilization of the benzyl carbocation, the hydrolysis in polar aqueous medium follows the \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism.

answer.text: Any of the above two depending upon the temperature of reaction

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q24 - Identification of asymmetric carbons in tartaric acid derivative

questiontext.text: Which of the carbon atoms present in the molecule given below are asymmetric?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An asymmetric (chiral) carbon atom is a tetrahedral \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridized carbon atom bonded to four distinctly different atoms or groups of atoms.

Step 2: Evaluation of Each Carbon Atom
- Carbon a: Part of a carboxylic acid group (\(\mathrm{-COOH}\)), bonded to an oxygen with a double bond; it is \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridized with only three attached groups, so it is achiral.
- Carbon b: Bonded to four different substituents: \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-COOH}\), and \(\mathrm{-CH(OH)COOH}\). Therefore, carbon b is asymmetric.
- Carbon c: Bonded to four different substituents: \(\mathrm{-H}\), \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-COOH}\), and \(\mathrm{-CH(OH)COOH}\). Therefore, carbon c is asymmetric.
- Carbon d: Part of a carboxylic acid group (\(\mathrm{-COOH}\)), \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridized with only three attached groups, so it is achiral.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only carbon atoms b and c are asymmetric.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q25 - Racemic mixture formation on nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text:
Which of the following compounds will give racemic mixture on nucleophilic substitution by \(\mathrm{OH}^{-}\) ion?

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Racemization occurs when nucleophilic substitution proceeds via an \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism at an optically active, chiral carbon centre. The departure of the leaving group yields a planar, achiral \(\mathrm{sp}^2\)-hybridized carbocation. The nucleophile can then attack with equal probability from either face of the planar carbocation, producing an equimolar mixture of enantiomers (a racemic mixture). If the starting substrate is achiral, the product remains achiral regardless of mechanism.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Given Compounds
- Compound (a) [2-bromobutane]: The carbon carrying bromine is attached to four distinct groups: \(\mathrm{-CH_3}\), \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\), \(\mathrm{-H}\), and \(\mathrm{-Br}\). It is an optically active chiral molecule. Ionization produces a planar carbocation, which on attack by \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) yields a racemic mixture of (+/-)-butan-2-ol.
- Compound (b) [1-bromobutane]: The carbon bonded to bromine is attached to two hydrogen atoms; it is achiral and substitution yields achiral butan-1-ol without racemization.
- Compound (c) [1-bromo-2-methylpropane]: The carbon bonded to bromine is attached to two hydrogen atoms; it is achiral and does not form a racemic mixture.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Only compound (a) produces a racemic mixture upon nucleophilic substitution by hydroxide ion.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q26 - Rate of nucleophilic aromatic substitution with nitro group

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution:

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic aromatic substitution in haloarenes occurs via an addition-elimination mechanism involving a negatively charged Meisenheimer complex intermediate. Electron-withdrawing groups such as \(\mathrm{-NO}_2\) at ortho and para positions strongly stabilize the carbanion intermediate by resonance (-R) and inductive (-I) effects, dramatically increasing the reaction rate relative to unsubstituted chlorobenzene.

Step 2: Comparison of the Substituted Haloarenes
- In chlorobenzene (a), no electron-withdrawing nitro group is present, making it the least reactive.
- In 2-nitrochlorobenzene (c), the nitro group is ortho to the chlorine atom. Although the electronic stabilization of the carbanion is strong, steric hindrance near the reaction site slightly retards nucleophilic attack compared to the para isomer.
- In 4-nitrochlorobenzene (b), the nitro group is para to chlorine, providing powerful resonance stabilization without any steric hindrance at the reaction centre, giving the fastest rate.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The rate of nucleophilic substitution increases in the order: \((\mathrm{a}) < (\mathrm{c}) < (\mathrm{b})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q27 - Influence of electron-releasing methyl group on nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution:

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic aromatic substitution proceeds via a carbanionic Meisenheimer intermediate. Electron-donating groups like methyl (\(\mathrm{-CH}_3\)) donate electron density via inductive (+I) and hyperconjugative effects, which destabilizes the negatively charged intermediate and decreases the rate of nucleophilic substitution. In addition, ortho substituents exert steric hindrance to incoming nucleophiles.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- In 2-chlorotoluene (b), the methyl group is located ortho to chlorine. It destabilizes the transition state both electronically and sterically, leading to the slowest rate of substitution.
- In 3-chlorotoluene (c), the methyl group is meta to chlorine. Electron donation by hyperconjugation does not deliver electron density directly to the ipso carbon, but its +I effect still destabilizes the intermediate relative to unsubstituted chlorobenzene, making it intermediate in rate.
- In chlorobenzene (a), there is no electron-donating methyl group to destabilize the carbanion intermediate, so it reacts fastest among the three.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The rate of nucleophilic substitution increases in the order: \((\mathrm{b}) < (\mathrm{c}) < (\mathrm{a})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q28 - Effect of multiple nitro groups on nucleophilic aromatic substitution

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution:

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Nucleophilic aromatic substitution involves the formation of a negatively charged \(\sigma\)-complex (Meisenheimer intermediate). Strong electron-withdrawing groups (\(\mathrm{-NO}_2\)) located at ortho and para positions relative to the halogen withdrawal electron density through powerful resonance (-R) and inductive (-I) effects, stabilizing the carbanionic transition state. Greater numbers of nitro groups at these positions lead to drastically increased substitution rates.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- Chlorobenzene (a) contains no electron-withdrawing groups; the ring is unactivated and substitution occurs only under drastically forcing conditions.
- 4-Nitrochlorobenzene (b) has one nitro group at the para position, activating the ring and permitting reaction under milder conditions.
- 2,4,6-Trinitrochlorobenzene (picryl chloride) (c) has three nitro groups (two ortho and one para) stabilizing the intermediate so strongly that substitution occurs readily even with warm water.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The rate of nucleophilic substitution increases in the order: \((\mathrm{a}) < (\mathrm{b}) < (\mathrm{c})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q29 - Retarding effect of multiple methyl groups on nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of rate of reaction towards nucleophilic substitution:

(a)

(b)

(c)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Electron-donating methyl groups (\(\mathrm{-CH}_3\)) donate electrons via inductive (+I) and hyperconjugative effects, which destabilizes the carbanionic intermediate formed during nucleophilic aromatic substitution and increases the electron density on the aromatic ring, repelling incoming nucleophiles. In addition, methyl groups adjacent to the reaction site introduce significant steric hindrance. Consequently, each additional electron-donating methyl group progressively lowers the rate of substitution.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- The dimethyl-substituted chlorobenzene (c) has two electron-donating methyl groups that maximize destabilization of the anionic transition state and create steric crowding, making it the least reactive.
- 4-Chlorotoluene (b) has one electron-releasing methyl group that retards substitution compared to unsubstituted chlorobenzene, giving it intermediate reactivity.
- Chlorobenzene (a) contains no electron-donating substituents, and therefore reacts at the highest rate among the three compounds.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The rate of nucleophilic substitution increases in the order: \((\mathrm{c}) < (\mathrm{b}) < (\mathrm{a})\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q30 - Increasing order of boiling points for butane and butyl halides

questiontext.text:
Which is the correct increasing order of boiling points of the following compounds?

1-Iodobutane, 1-Bromobutane, 1-Chlorobutane, Butane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boiling points of organic compounds depend on the strength of intermolecular attractive forces. For haloalkanes of the same alkyl group, intermolecular dipole-dipole interactions and London dispersion forces increase systematically with an increase in the size and polarizability of the halogen atom and the overall molecular mass.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- Unsubstituted butane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_{10}\)) is non-polar and exhibits only weak dispersion forces with a low molecular mass (\(58\text{ g/mol}\)), giving it the lowest boiling point.
- For the 1-halobutanes, halogen size, polarizability, and molecular weight increase in the sequence \(\mathrm{Cl} < \mathrm{Br} < \mathrm{I}\). As a result, dispersion forces strengthen in the order: 1-chlorobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Cl}\)) < 1-bromobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Br}\)) < 1-iodobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{I}\)).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of boiling points is: Butane < 1-Chlorobutane < 1-Bromobutane < 1-Iodobutane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q31 - Increasing order of boiling points of bromo derivatives

questiontext.text:
Which is the correct increasing order of boiling points of the following compounds?

1-Bromoethane, 1-Bromopropane, 1-Bromobutane, Bromobenzene

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The boiling point of homologous halogenated compounds increases with increasing chain length and molecular mass because London dispersion forces scale directly with molecular surface area and the total number of polarizable electrons. In addition, aromatic haloarenes possess a large planar \(\pi\)-electron cloud with high polarizability, leading to particularly strong intermolecular dispersion forces.

Step 2: Comparison of the Compounds
- For the aliphatic bromoalkanes, the chain length increases from ethyl to propyl to butyl. Consequently, boiling point increases in the order: 1-bromoethane (\(\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(109\text{ g/mol}\)) < 1-bromopropane (\(\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_7\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(123\text{ g/mol}\)) < 1-bromobutane (\(\mathrm{C}_4\mathrm{H}_9\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(137\text{ g/mol}\)).
- Bromobenzene (\(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{Br}\), molar mass \(157\text{ g/mol}\)) has the highest molecular mass and a large planar delocalized aromatic ring, imparting the strongest dispersion interactions and the highest boiling point.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct increasing order of boiling points is: 1-Bromoethane < 1-Bromopropane < 1-Bromobutane < Bromobenzene.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q32 - Nature of nucleophiles and hybridisation in bimolecular transition state

questiontext.text:
Consider the following reaction and answer the question:

Which of the statements are correct about above reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reaction depicted is a bimolecular nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)) process. In this concerted pathway, the attacking species is a nucleophile and the leaving group is also displaced as a nucleophile. The transition state involves simultaneous partial bond making and bond breaking.

Step 2: Identification of Species and Hybridisation
- Species (a) is the hydroxide ion (\(\mathrm{OH}^-\)), which acts as the incoming nucleophile by donating a pair of electrons. Species (e) is the displaced chloride ion (\(\mathrm{Cl}^-\)), which departs carrying a pair of electrons, functioning as a leaving nucleophile. Therefore, both (a) and (e) are nucleophiles.
- In the pentacoordinated transition state (c), the central carbon atom is bonded to three equatorial substituents via coplanar \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybrid orbitals separated by approximately \(120^\circ\), while the incoming nucleophile and departing leaving group interact via a perpendicular axial p-orbital. Hence, the central carbon in the transition state is \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridized.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that (a) and (e) are both nucleophiles, and in (c) the carbon atom is \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) hybridised.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q33 - Stereochemistry and mechanism of bimolecular substitution

questiontext.text:
Consider the reaction:

Which of the following statements are correct about this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The single-step reaction involves backside nucleophilic attack by hydroxide ion on the substrate with concerted expulsion of chloride ion via a pentacoordinate transition state. This mechanism is defined as \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) (substitution nucleophilic bimolecular).

Step 2: Stereochemical Analysis
Backside attack causes the three non-reacting groups attached to the asymmetric carbon to flip over to the opposite side like an umbrella in a gale, resulting in complete stereochemical inversion (Walden inversion). Therefore, substrate (b) and product (d) have opposite configurations.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that the reaction proceeds via the \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism, and the substrate (b) and product (d) have opposite stereochemical configurations.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q34 - Stability of transition state in bimolecular nucleophilic substitution

questiontext.text: Which of the following statements are correct about the reaction intermediate/transition state (c) in the reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) pathway, species (c) represents a transition state (energy maximum on the reaction coordinate), not a stable isolable intermediate. The transition state features partial bonding to both the incoming nucleophile and the leaving group.

Step 2: Evaluation of Transition State Stability
In the transition state (c), the central carbon atom is simultaneously coordinated to five groups (three normal covalent bonds in the equatorial plane and two partial axial bonds). This pentacoordinate arrangement results in considerable steric crowding, non-ideal bond angles, and high electrostatic repulsion. Consequently, the transition state lies at a potential energy maximum and is far less stable than the reactant (b).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that intermediate/transition state (c) is unstable because the carbon atom is attached to 5 atoms, and it is less stable than reactant (b).

answer.text: Intermediate (c) is unstable because in this carbon is attached to 5 atoms.
Intermediate (c) is unstable because carbon atom is \(sp^2\) hybridised.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q35 - Mechanism of bimolecular substitution of secondary haloalkane

questiontext.text:
Answer the question on the basis of the following reaction:

Which of the following statements are correct about the mechanism of this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) substitution process occurs via a concerted, synchronous mechanism rather than through sequential steps involving a free carbocation.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Mechanism
- Nucleophilic attack by \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) occurs from the backside opposite to the leaving group \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\). As the \(\mathrm{C-OH}\) bond begins to form, the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond simultaneously weakens and begins to break. Therefore, \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) attaches to substrate (b) from one side and \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) leaves simultaneously from the other side.
- The transition state (c) has partially formed and partially broken bonds that are weaker than standard covalent bonds, representing an unstable high-energy state.
- A carbocation intermediate is not formed in this concerted bimolecular mechanism.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that \(\mathrm{OH}^-\) attaches to the substrate from one side while \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) leaves simultaneously from the opposite side, and the transition state is an unstable state with weak bonds.

\(\mathrm{OH}^-\) attaches to the substrate (b) from one side and \(\mathrm{Cl}^-\) leaves simultaneously from other side.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q36 - Reaction kinetics and molecularity of bimolecular substitution

questiontext.text:
Answer the question on the basis of the following reaction:

Which of the following statements are correct about the kinetics of this reaction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The reaction proceeds by an \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) mechanism, which takes place in a single elementary step involving both the alkyl halide substrate and the nucleophile in the rate-determining transition state.

Step 2: Kinetics and Molecularity
- The rate law is second-order overall, first-order with respect to the substrate (b) and first-order with respect to the nucleophile (a):
\[ \text{Rate} = k\,[\text{a}][\text{b}] \]
Thus, the rate of reaction depends on the concentration of both (a) and (b).
- Because two colliding reactant molecules participate in forming the transition state of this single elementary step, the molecularity of the reaction is two.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that the rate of reaction depends on the concentration of both (a) and (b), and the molecularity of the reaction is two.

answer.text: The rate of reaction depends only on the concentration of (b).
The rate of reaction depends on the concentration of both (a) and (b).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q37 - Identification of haloalkanes with sp3 hybridized carbon

questiontext.text: Haloalkanes contain halogen atom(s) attached to the \(sp^3\) hybridised carbon atom of an alkyl group. Identify haloalkane from the following compounds.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Haloalkanes (alkyl halides) are aliphatic halogenated derivatives where the halogen atom is bonded directly to an \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridized carbon atom belonging to a saturated aliphatic alkyl chain or saturated carbon skeleton.

Step 2: Structural Analysis of the Compounds
- 2-Bromopentane: Structure is \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Br})\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\). The bromine atom is bonded to a secondary saturated \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridized carbon of an alkyl group; hence, it is a haloalkane.
- Vinyl chloride: Structure is \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH-Cl}\). The chlorine atom is attached to an \(\mathrm{sp}^2\)-hybridized vinylic carbon atom; hence, it is a vinylic halide, not a haloalkane.
- Chloroethene: IUPAC name for vinyl chloride (\(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH-Cl}\)); the chlorine atom is attached to an \(\mathrm{sp}^2\)-hybridized alkene carbon atom.
- Trichloromethane (chloroform): Structure is \(\mathrm{CHCl}_3\). Three chlorine atoms are attached to an \(\mathrm{sp}^3\)-hybridized carbon atom of a methane-derived alkyl framework; hence, it is a polyhaloalkane.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The compounds that are haloalkanes are 2-bromopentane and trichloromethane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q38 - Properties and reactions of ethylene and ethylidene chloride isomers

questiontext.text: Ethylene chloride and ethylidene chloride are isomers. Identify the correct statements.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Ethylene chloride (1,2-dichloroethane, \(\mathrm{ClCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}\)) is a vicinal dihalide, whereas ethylidene chloride (1,1-dichloroethane, \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHCl}_2\)) is a geminal dihalide. Because their chlorine atoms are positioned differently on the carbon chain, they are positional isomers, not chain isomers.

Step 2: Analysis of the Chemical Reactions
- Dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\): Both undergo two successive \(\beta\)-elimination reactions of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to yield the same alkyne, ethyne (\(\mathrm{CH}\equiv\mathrm{CH}\)):
\[ \mathrm{ClCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl} + 2\,\text{alc. }\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} + 2\,\mathrm{KCl} + 2\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]
\[ \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHCl}_2 + 2\,\text{alc. }\mathrm{KOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HC}\equiv\mathrm{CH} + 2\,\mathrm{KCl} + 2\,\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]
Thus, both form ethyne with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\).
- Reduction: Complete reduction with zinc and hydrochloric acid or \(\mathrm{H}_2/\mathrm{Ni}\) removes both chlorine atoms, yielding the parent alkane, ethane (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}_3\)), from both isomers.
- Hydrolysis with aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\): Ethylene chloride gives ethane-1,2-diol (glycol), whereas ethylidene chloride gives ethanal (acetaldehyde), producing different products upon hydrolysis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that both compounds form ethyne on treatment with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\), and both form ethane on reduction.

answer.text: Both compounds form ethyne on treatment with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\).
Both compounds form the same product on treatment with aqueous \(\mathrm{KOH}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q39 - Identification of geminal dihalides

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds are gem-dihalides?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Geminal dihalides (gem-dihalides) are dihalogenated organic derivatives in which both halogen atoms are bonded to the same carbon atom. In contrast, vicinal dihalides (vic-dihalides) have the two halogen atoms bonded to adjacent carbon atoms.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Structures
- Ethylidene chloride: Structure is \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHCl}_2\). Both chlorine atoms are attached to carbon-1; hence, it is a gem-dihalide.
- Ethylene dichloride: Structure is \(\mathrm{ClCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}\). The two chlorine atoms are attached to adjacent carbon atoms (C-1 and C-2); hence, it is a vic-dihalide.
- Methylene chloride: Structure is \(\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}_2\). Both chlorine atoms are attached to the single methane carbon atom; hence, it is a gem-dihalide.
- Benzyl chloride: Structure is \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Cl}\). It is a monohalogenated benzylic compound, not a dihalide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The compounds that are gem-dihalides are ethylidene chloride and methylene chloride.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q40 - Classification of secondary alkyl bromides

questiontext.text: Which of the following are secondary bromides?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
An alkyl halide is classified as secondary (\(2^\circ\)) if the carbon atom directly bonded to the halogen atom is attached to exactly two other carbon atoms and one hydrogen atom.

Step 2: Evaluation of the Structures
- \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CHBr}\) (2-bromopropane): The \(\mathrm{-CH(Br)-}\) carbon is attached to two methyl carbon atoms; hence, it is a secondary bromide.
- \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_3\mathrm{CCH}_2\mathrm{Br}\) (1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane / neopentyl bromide): The \(\mathrm{-CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\) carbon is attached to only one quaternary carbon atom; hence, it is a primary (\(1^\circ\)) bromide.
- \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Br})\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) (2-bromobutane): The \(\mathrm{-CH(Br)-}\) carbon is attached to a methyl group and an ethyl group (two carbon atoms); hence, it is a secondary bromide.
- \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CBrCH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\) (2-bromo-2-methylbutane): The bromine-bearing carbon is attached to three other carbon atoms; hence, it is a tertiary (\(3^\circ\)) bromide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The secondary bromides are \((\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{CHBr}\) and \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{Br})\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q41 - Classification of aryl halides with ring-bound halogen

questiontext.text: Which of the following compounds can be classified as aryl halides?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Aryl halides (haloarenes) are compounds in which the halogen atom is directly bonded to an \(\mathrm{sp}^2\)-hybridized carbon atom of an aromatic ring.

Step 2: Structural Analysis
- In \(p\text{-ClC}_6\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\), the chlorine atom is directly attached to the benzene ring at the position para to an isobutyl group; hence, it is an aryl halide.
- In \(p\text{-CH}_3\mathrm{CHCl}(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_4)\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\), the chlorine atom is attached to an \(\mathrm{sp}^3\) side-chain benzylic carbon rather than directly to the ring; hence, it is a benzylic halide.
- In \(o\text{-BrH}_2\mathrm{C - C}_6\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}_3\), the bromine atom is bonded to a side-chain \(\mathrm{-CH}_2-\) carbon; hence, it is a benzylic halide.
- In \(\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{-Cl}\) (chlorobenzene), the chlorine atom is bonded directly to the \(\mathrm{sp}^2\) carbon of the benzene ring; hence, it is an aryl halide.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The compounds classified as aryl halides are \(p\text{-ClC}_6\mathrm{H}_4\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\) and \(\mathrm{C_6H_5 - Cl}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q42 - Reagents for preparing alkyl halides from alcohols

questiontext.text: Alkyl halides are prepared from alcohols by treating with

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Alcohols can be converted into alkyl halides by replacing the hydroxyl (\(\mathrm{-OH}\)) group with a halogen using halogen acids, phosphorus halides, or thionyl chloride.

Step 2: Evaluation of Reagents
- \(\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{ZnCl}_2\) (Groove's process / Lucas reagent): Anhydrous \(\mathrm{ZnCl}_2\) coordinates with the alcohol oxygen to weaken the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond, enabling chloride ion substitution to produce alkyl chlorides. Thus, this is a valid method.
- \(\text{Red }\mathrm{P} + \mathrm{Br}_2\): Generates phosphorus tribromide (\(\mathrm{PBr}_3\)) in situ, which readily converts alcohols into the corresponding alkyl bromides (\(3\mathrm{ROH} + \mathrm{PBr}_3 \longrightarrow 3\mathrm{RBr} + \mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_3\)). Thus, this is a valid method.
- \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 + \mathrm{KI}\): Sulfuric acid is a strong oxidizing agent; it oxidizes the in situ formed \(\mathrm{HI}\) into elemental iodine (\(\mathrm{I}_2\)):
\[ 2\mathrm{HI} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4 \longrightarrow \mathrm{I}_2 + \mathrm{SO}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \]
As a result, \(\mathrm{HI}\) is not available to react with the alcohol, preventing alkyl iodide formation. Non-oxidizing phosphoric acid (\(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{PO}_4\)) must be used instead.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Alkyl halides can be prepared from alcohols using \(\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{ZnCl}_2\) and \(\text{Red }\mathrm{P} + \mathrm{Br}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HALOALKANES_AND_HALOARENES_MCQ_Q43 - Inorganic fluorides used in Swarts reaction

questiontext.text: Alkyl fluorides are synthesised by heating an alkyl chloride/bromide in presence of ________ or ________.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The synthesis of alkyl fluorides by halogen exchange from alkyl chlorides or bromides is known as the Swarts reaction. Heating the alkyl chloride/bromide in the presence of heavy metal fluorides facilitates the substitution of the halide by fluorine.

Step 2: Suitable Metallic Fluorides
Standard metallic fluorides utilized for the Swarts reaction include silver fluoride (\(\mathrm{AgF}\)), mercurous fluoride (\(\mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2\)), cobalt(II) fluoride (\(\mathrm{CoF}_2\)), and antimony trifluoride (\(\mathrm{SbF}_3\)).
In contrast, ionic alkali/alkaline-earth fluorides such as \(\mathrm{NaF}\) and \(\mathrm{CaF}_2\) are not suitable for this transformation due to high lattice enthalpy and unfavourable solubility.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The appropriate metallic fluorides among the choices are \(\mathrm{CoF}_2\) and \(\mathrm{Hg}_2\mathrm{F}_2\).
